text: The GeForce 400 series is a line of graphics processing units developed by Nvidia, marking the debut of the Fermi microarchitecture. Originally scheduled for release in November 2009, it was delayed and launched on March 26, 2010, with availability beginning in April 2010. Its primary competitor was ATI's Radeon HD 5000 series. Nvidia positioned the Fermi architecture as the next major advancement after the Tesla architecture used in the G80, with the GF100 being the first Fermi-based chip featuring 512 stream processors organized into sixteen groups of 32 and 3.0 billion transistors, manufactured using a 40 nm process by TSMC. The GF100 supports OpenGL 4.0 and Direct3D 11, but no fully enabled GF100 GPUs were sold; the GTX 480 had one streaming multiprocessor disabled, the GTX 470 had two streaming multiprocessors and one memory controller disabled, and the GTX 465 had five streaming multiprocessors and two memory controllers disabled. Consumer GeForce cards included 256MB of GDDR5 memory per enabled memory controller, resulting in total memory capacities of 1.5GB, 1.25GB, or 1.0GB, while the Tesla C2050 had 512MB per controller on six controllers and the Tesla C2070 had 1024MB per controller, both with fourteen active stream processor groups. Tesla cards support optional ECC memory and perform one double-precision floating-point operation per cycle per core, whereas consumer GeForce cards are driver-restricted to one double-precision operation per four cycles. These features, along with support for Visual Studio and C++, target professional and commercial markets and high-performance computing. The Fermi name honors Italian physicist Enrico Fermi. Despite an increase in L2 cache from 256kB per 240 ALUs to 768kB per 512 ALUs, the on-board SRAM per ALU decreased due to fewer registers (32,768 per 32 ALUs vs. 16,384 per 8 ALUs), less shared memory (48kB per 32 ALUs vs. 16kB per 8 ALUs), and reduced cache (16kB per 32 ALUs vs. 8kB constant cache per 8 ALUs plus 24kB texture cache per 24 ALUs). A white paper released on September 30, 2009, detailed the architecture: 16 Streaming Multiprocessors, each with 32 CUDA Cores capable of one single-precision operation per cycle or one double-precision operation every other cycle, a 40-bit virtual address space enabling direct host memory mapping, and a 384-bit GDDR5 memory interface. Threads are scheduled in warps of 32 threads per shader core. The GF100 features 64 KB of shared memory per cluster, configurable as 48 KB cache plus 16 KB shared memory or 16 KB cache plus 48 KB shared memory, along with a 768 KB L2 cache shared across all 16 clusters. The white paper emphasized the chip as a general-purpose processor for workloads involving tens of thousands of threads, similar to the Tera MTA architecture but lacking efficient random memory access. Users reported high temperatures and power consumption with minimal performance gains over AMD's Radeon HD 5000 series, prompting AMD to release a promotional video titled "The Misunderstanding" that humorously depicted a police raid on a house with a high thermal profile, revealing the source as a Fermi GPU, a joke that popularized the idea of frying an egg on a Fermi GPU at full load. All products in the series use a 40 nm fabrication process and support Direct3D 12.0 at feature level 11.0, OpenGL 4.6, and OpenCL 1.1, except the GeForce 405, an OEM-only card based on the GT218 (Tesla) core that supports only DirectX 11.1 at feature level 10.1, OpenGL 3.3, and lacks OpenCL support—making it the only GeForce 400 series card not based on the Fermi architecture. The GeForce 405 is functionally identical to the GeForce 310, which itself is based on the GeForce 210. All cards have a single DB15 VGA connector on full-height, full-length cards, except as noted. On November 8, 2010, Nvidia released the GF110 chip and the GTX 580, a redesigned GF100 with significantly reduced power consumption, enabling all 16 streaming multiprocessors. Features of the full GF100 architecture were only available on Quadro and Tesla cards; consumer GeForce cards have only a quarter of the double-precision performance and lack ECC memory. The GF100 provides Compute Capability 2.0, while GF104/106/108 offer Compute Capability 2.1. Nvidia ceased releasing 32-bit drivers for 32-bit operating systems starting with driver release 390. In April 2018, Nvidia announced that Fermi would transition to legacy driver support and remain supported until January 2019.
